newsitem.title: USA: American sees Heathrow slots opening up.
newsitem.headline: American sees Heathrow slots opening up.

text.p: Upon the completion of a new Anglo-U.S. air treaty, "more than enough slots" would be available at London's Heathrow Airport to satisfy a recent proposal by the U.S. General Accounting Office, American Airlines said on Thursday.
The GAO on Wednesday outlined a plan under which six U.S. airlines that do not currently serve Heathrow should obtain enough slots to operate 23 daily round-trip flights.

Several U.S. carriers have criticized the proposed alliance between AMR Corp's American Airlines and British Airways Plc, saying the combination would dominate trans-Atlantic air travel and lead to higher fares.
Landing rights at crowded Heathrow have become a key issue in the debate. Critics of the alliance contend that there are no slots available at the airport to allow new airlines to provide service.

American said it was "pleased that the GAO found that the slots for these 23 new daily services need not come from American and British Airways, but could come from three sources: new slot creation, exchanges between alliance partners and purchases from other airlines."
The GAO, however, said there are some practical obstacles to obtaining slots at Heathrow.

"As a practical matter, therefore, in addition to acquiring some slots under current procedures, the six U.S. airlines will likely need to have slots transferred to them from American Airlines and British Airways," the GAO said.
American has said previously that it and British Airways were prepared to sell enough slots to operate 12 daily round trips, if necessary.

On Thursday, American said that more than 23 slots would be available to satisfy the GAO requirement, without divestiture from American or BA. American said the largest source of slots would be the creation of new ones.

American cited a forecast by BAA Plc, which operates Heathrow. BAA expects increased airport and airspace efficiency would create 20 to 29 peak-hour round-trip slots by the end of 1998, American said in a prepared statement.
The GAO, a congressional arm, also said the potential alliance of American and BA, the two largest carriers in the U.S.-British market, "raises significant competition issues."
American and BA announced a year ago that they planned an alliance to market each other's flights as their own and would seek antitrust immunity to do so.

The U.S. Department of Transportation has a policy of approving such alliances only if there is an "open skies" agreement allowing liberal access for airlines flying between the United States and the countries involved.
